# SPEC — corv32

Status: v1, Step 1/2 (Architect, 2026-10-04). DESIGN.md holds the exact interfaces.
Any later change to a claim, a threshold, a check list or a measurement procedure goes
in §8 (change log) and in docs/DECISIONS.md with a reason. Thresholds are fixed now,
before any RTL exists. Adjusting them after seeing results counts as narrowing the claim
and must be reported as such in the paper.

## 1. What corv32 is

A from-scratch, in-order, five-stage (IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB) RV32IM core with machine-mode
traps and interrupts, written in a Yosys- and Verilator-compatible SystemVerilog subset,
plus a small SoC (boot ROM, RAM, CLINT timer, 16550-subset UART, GPIO, SPI-flash boot)
and a Verilator model. No code is taken from any existing core. PicoRV32 and VexRiscv are
used only as measured baselines (third_party/, syn/, experiments/).

## 2. Claims

Prior-art review (docs/PRIOR_ART.md §5) found that every ingredient of the brief's claim
is routine, that ≥ 2 CoreMark/MHz is a low bar for a five-stage RV32IM core, and that
two unreviewed public repositories already claim the whole combination. So the brief's
claim becomes the **engineering acceptance gate (E1)**. The paper's research claim is the
**verification-yield study (C1)**. C2 and C3 are supporting measurements.

### C1 — primary research claim (verification yield)

> Take the pre-registered bug corpus B. B is (i) 200 single-point mutants of corv32's
> non-RVFI core RTL, generated by Yosys `mutate` with seed 1 by the procedure in
> DESIGN §9.6, and (ii) the 20 hand-written bugs listed in DESIGN §9.6, committed before
> any of them is evaluated. Let K ⊆ B be the killable bugs: bugs killed by at least one
> method, plus survivors that manual triage classifies as architecturally visible. Four
> methods are each run to completion on every bug in B: M_dir (core-level cocotb directed
> tests), M_act (RISCOF with riscv-arch-test 3.9.1), M_fv (riscv-formal BMC at the
> DESIGN §9.2 depths) and M_ls (Spike lockstep over the fixed ≥ 1,000,000-instruction
> random-program campaign). Then all three of the following hold:
> (a) M_fv kills at least 80% of K;
> (b) no single method kills all of K, and at least 5% of K is killed by a
> simulation-based method (M_dir, M_act or M_ls) but not by M_fv;
> (c) the union of the four methods kills all 20 hand-written bugs.
>
> **Refuted if** M_fv kills fewer than 80% of K, or one method alone kills all of K, or
> fewer than 5% of K are killed by simulation but missed by M_fv, or any hand-written bug
> survives all four methods.

Why these thresholds, fixed before measurement:
- (a) 80%: riscv-formal checks every RV32IM instruction from unconstrained states, under
  random bus stalls and random interrupts. Under `RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS` it does **not** see
  the real multiplier or divider datapath, and those are roughly 10–20% of core logic
  (DESIGN §11 budget). So the expected yield is high but clearly below 100%. A value
  under 80% would mean riscv-formal is much weaker on a pipelined core than its design
  intent suggests. Funck et al. (FDL 2023) report holes, but give no rate we could reuse.
- (b) 5%: this is the M-datapath share above, cut by a safety factor. It is the
  quantitative form of "formal and simulation are complementary".
- (c) This is a sanity floor for the whole verification stack. Each hand-written bug
  models a realistic design error (DESIGN §9.6).

Reported but not thresholded: kill rate per method, the full bug × method kill matrix,
unique kills per method, time to first kill (CPU-seconds), and instructions or BMC depth
at the kill.

### E1 — engineering acceptance gate (the brief's claim, made exact)

> corv32 (DESIGN default parameters: FORWARDING=1, MUL_FAST=1, REDIRECT_REG=0)
> 1. passes every riscv-formal check in the list of DESIGN §9.2 (`isa rv32im`, NRET=1,
>    XLEN=32, ILEN=32, `RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS`, `RISCV_FORMAL_ALIGNED_MEM`) as a bounded model
>    check at the listed depths, under SymbiYosys from the pinned OSS CAD Suite;
> 2. passes all RISCOF tests that riscv-arch-test 3.9.1 selects for corv32's ISA YAML from
>    `rv32i_m/{I, M, Zifencei, privilege}` (63 tests expected: 39 + 8 + 1 + 15), with
>    every signature equal to Spike's;
> 3. matches Spike (pinned riscv-isa-sim 609dbe0) commit for commit, with 0 mismatches,
>    on ≥ 1,000,000 compared retired instructions from the random-program campaign of
>    DESIGN §9.4. A commit matches when pc, instruction word, rd write, memory address,
>    store data and trap cause/epc/tval are all equal;
> 4. scores ≥ 2.00 CoreMark/MHz by the measurement defined in §3.
>
> **Refuted (gate failed) if** any listed check reports FAIL or ERROR, any selected
> RISCOF test fails or is not run, any lockstep mismatch is attributable to the DUT (a
> mismatch is attributable to the DUT unless it is in the pre-declared exclusion list of
> DESIGN §9.4), fewer than 1,000,000 instructions are compared, CoreMark self-validation
> fails, or the measured value is below 2.00.

### C2 — supporting result: same-FPGA, same-flow baseline comparison (reported)

corv32, PicoRV32 (two configurations) and VexRiscv (three pregenerated variants) are
synthesised core-only on a Lattice ECP5 LFE5U-25F-6 (CABGA381), with identical Yosys
0.69 `synth_ecp5` and nextpnr-ecp5 settings and 10 placement seeds each. For every
design we report median, min and max Fmax, LUT4, FF, LUTRAM, DP16KD and MULT18X18D, and
CoreMark/MHz from the same binary in the same simulation harness (DESIGN §10, §12). No
pass/fail threshold applies. The table compares, it is not a contest.

### C3 — supporting result: cost of reaching 2 CoreMark/MHz (reported, with predictions)

There are 2³ = 8 configurations of {FORWARDING, MUL_FAST, REDIRECT_REG}. For each we
report CoreMark/MHz, LUT4, FF, DSP, Fmax (10 seeds) and CoreMark/s = CoreMark/MHz × median
Fmax. The predictions, registered now from the DESIGN §7.8 CPI model:
- (P1) every configuration with FORWARDING=0 scores below 2.00;
- (P2) the default configuration has the highest CoreMark/MHz.
These are predictions. If one fails, we report it as a finding. E1 does not depend on it.

## 3. How "CoreMark/MHz" is measured (normative)

- Source: eembc/coremark @ 1f483d5, unmodified except the `core_portme.{c,h,mak}` files
  in `sw/coremark/`. These are allowed by the run rules.
- Compiler: xPack riscv-none-elf-gcc 15.2.0-1. Flags (fixed):
  `-O2 -march=rv32im_zicsr -mabi=ilp32 -ffreestanding -fno-common -nostdlib -nostartfiles`
  `-DPERFORMANCE_RUN=1 -DITERATIONS=<n>`, linked with libgcc, `-T sw/common/link.ld`
  (code and data in RAM at 0x8000_0000). As a secondary result only, we also report
  `-O3 -funroll-loops`. Prior art shows flags alone move CoreMark/MHz by up to 1.5×
  (Gallmann, CARRV 2021).
- Platform: cycle-accurate Verilator 5.053 simulation of `corv32_soc` (DESIGN §8). The
  core fetches from and loads/stores to on-chip dual-port RAM with zero wait states (one
  cycle of synchronous latency, one access per cycle per port).
- Timer: `get_time()` reads the CLINT `mtime` register (0x0200_BFF8). In the measurement
  build `mtime` increments once per clock cycle. `EE_TICKS_PER_SEC` = 1,000,000, so
  CoreMark's own "Iterations/Sec" output equals CoreMark/MHz.
- Metric: **CoreMark/MHz = ITERATIONS × 10⁶ / (mtime at stop_time − mtime at
  start_time)**. This counts only cycles inside CoreMark's timed region.
- Validation: the run must print "Correct operation validated". We also run the
  validation seed set (0x3415,0x3415,0x66), and it must validate too.
- Run length: EEMBC requires ≥ 10 s of run time, which simulation cannot give in wall-clock
  terms. We set ITERATIONS so that the timed cycle count, divided by corv32's median
  Fmax from M6, is ≥ 10 s of *simulated* time. Default ITERATIONS = 3000, which is
  ≥ 10 s for Fmax up to about 130 MHz at 2.3 CoreMark/MHz. The value used is reported. We
  also run with ITERATIONS = 10 and report the difference, which should be < 0.5%. The
  result is labelled "CoreMark/MHz measured in RTL simulation; not an EEMBC-certified
  score". The report line uses the README format: `CoreMark/MHz 1.0 : N / GCC 15.2.0
  <flags> / Heap? no / RAM`.
- Variance: Verilator simulation of this design is deterministic, so one run per
  configuration is enough. A second run must reproduce the same cycle count, or that is
  treated as a bug.
- Baselines: the same ELF runs in per-baseline Verilator harnesses (DESIGN §12.2). Each
  baseline gets an ideal memory that answers in the fastest way its own protocol allows,
  which favours the baselines. These numbers are context, not part of E1.

## 4. Scope (normative)

### 4.1 ISA
RV32I + M + Zicsr + Zicntr + Zifencei, machine mode only (no U, no S, no debug mode).
`misa` = 0x4000_1100 (MXL=1, I, M), read-only. The GCC string is
`rv32im_zicsr_zifencei`. The Spike string is `rv32im_zicsr_zicntr_zifencei` with
`--priv=m`. Not implemented: C, A, F/D, B, PMP, hpm counters (read as zero),
Zihpm, Smcntrpmf, Sstc, debug.

### 4.2 CSRs
Accessing any CSR not listed here raises illegal instruction. So does a write
attempt (CSRRW/CSRRWI always, CSRRS/C with rs1 field ≠ 0) to a read-only address
(addr[11:10] = 2'b11).

| addr | name | behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| 0x300 | mstatus | MIE[3], MPIE[7] RW; MPP[12:11] reads 2'b11; all else 0 |
| 0x301 | misa | 0x4000_1100; writes ignored |
| 0x304 | mie | MSIE[3], MTIE[7], MEIE[11] RW; others 0 |
| 0x305 | mtvec | writes store `wdata & ~32'h2`; MODE bit0: 0 direct, 1 vectored (interrupts → base + 4·code) |
| 0x310 | mstatush | 0, writes ignored |
| 0x320 | mcountinhibit | 0, writes ignored (Spike differs; excluded from lockstep) |
| 0x323–0x33F | mhpmevent3–31 | 0, writes ignored (Spike stores them; excluded from lockstep) |
| 0x340 | mscratch | RW 32 bits |
| 0x341 | mepc | stores bits [31:1]; reads return bit1 and bit0 as 0 (IALIGN=32); RVFI reports the unmasked state |
| 0x342 | mcause | RW all 32 bits (WLRL, matches Spike) |
| 0x343 | mtval | RW 32 bits |
| 0x344 | mip | MSIP[3], MTIP[7], MEIP[11] read-only: the interrupt inputs registered once; writes ignored |
| 0xB00/0xB80 | mcycle/mcycleh | 64-bit RW, +1 every clock; a write overrides that cycle's increment |
| 0xB02/0xB82 | minstret/minstreth | 64-bit RW, +1 per retired instruction; a write overrides the writing instruction's own increment |
| 0xB03–0xB1F, 0xB83–0xB9F | mhpmcounter3–31(h) | 0, writes ignored |
| 0xC00/0xC80, 0xC02/0xC82 | cycle(h), instret(h) | read-only shadows of mcycle/minstret |
| 0xC01/0xC81 | time/timeh | read-only, the core's `mtime` input (CLINT) |
| 0xF11–0xF15 | mvendorid, marchid, mimpid, mhartid, mconfigptr | all read 0 (Spike's marchid = 5; excluded from lockstep) |
| 0x3A0–0x3EF, 0x7A0–0x7A3 | pmpcfg/pmpaddr, tselect/tdata | not implemented: illegal instruction (D12). Spike implements them (probe: `csrr pmpcfg0` reads 0x1f, `csrr tselect` reads 0), so the lockstep generator never emits them |

Reset values: mstatus.MIE = MPIE = 0, mie = 0, mtvec = 0, mepc = mcause = mtval =
mscratch = 0, mcycle = minstret = 0.

### 4.3 Instruction behaviours
- **FENCE**: no-op (one hart, in-order, no caches, no write buffer). Every encoding with
  opcode 0001111 and funct3 = 000 is legal, as in Spike.
- **FENCE.I**: legal for any opcode-0001111/funct3-001 encoding. It flushes the pipeline
  and refetches pc+4. A store older than the FENCE.I is visible to the refetch.
- **ECALL**: exception, mcause 11, mtval 0, mepc = pc.
- **EBREAK**: exception, mcause 3, mtval = pc, mepc = pc.
- **MRET**: pc ← mepc; MIE ← MPIE; MPIE ← 1.
- **WFI**: no-op. The privileged spec allows this. Spike is run with `--wfi-as-nop`.
- **Illegal**: mcause 2, mtval = the full 32-bit instruction word. (Spike reports only the
  low 16 bits when instruction bits [1:0] ≠ 11, e.g. 0xDEAD0001 gives mtval 0x0001, probed on
  the pinned Spike. The lockstep generator therefore keeps the upper half of such words 0,
  and `compare.py` compares them on the low half; D12.) The decoder accepts exactly the RV32IM,
  Zicsr, Zifencei, ECALL, EBREAK, MRET and WFI encodings (DESIGN §6.2). Everything else is
  illegal, including 0x0000_0000 and 0xFFFF_FFFF.

### 4.4 Memory and misalignment
Little-endian and byte-addressed. Bus addresses are word-aligned, with byte enables.
- Misaligned loads and stores are **not** supported. They trap: load address misaligned
  (4) or store address misaligned (6), mtval = the effective address, and no bus access is
  made. Spike traps on these too, because Zicclsm is absent from its ISA string.
- A taken branch, JAL or JALR whose target has bit1 set raises instruction address
  misaligned (0) on the jump itself. mtval = target, rd is not written. JALR clears target
  bit0 first.
- A bus error response raises an access fault: instruction (1, mtval = pc), load (5) or
  store (7), with mtval = the effective byte address. In the SoC, unmapped addresses
  return a bus error.

### 4.5 Traps and interrupts
- All exceptions are precise. mepc is the faulting instruction. No younger instruction
  has any architectural effect, and in particular no younger store reaches the bus.
- Interrupt inputs: `irq_external` (MEI, code 11), `irq_software` (MSI, code 3),
  `irq_timer` (MTI, code 7). They are level-sensitive and synchronous to `clk`. Priority
  is MEI > MSI > MTI. An interrupt is taken when mstatus.MIE = 1 and (mip & mie) ≠ 0.
  It is taken before an instruction executes; mepc = that instruction, mcause = 0x8000_0000
  | code, mtval = 0.
- On trap entry: MPIE ← MIE, MIE ← 0, pc ← handler. The handler is mtvec.BASE, or
  BASE + 4·code for interrupts when MODE = 1.
- Trapping instructions do not count toward minstret.
- Timer compare: the corv32 CLINT resets mtimecmp to all ones (no timer interrupt pending
  out of reset, DESIGN §8.2). Spike resets mtimecmp to 0, so MTIP is pending from reset
  there. The lockstep program writes mtimecmp = all ones first thing, which makes both
  models agree; a test that depends on the reset value must not be run in lockstep (D12).

### 4.6 Reset
Synchronous, active-high `rst`. The reset vector is the core parameter `RESET_ADDR`,
default 0x8000_0000. The SoC uses 0x0000_0000 (boot ROM), which copies a flash image to
RAM or falls through to 0x8000_0000 (DESIGN §8.3). Register-file contents are undefined
after reset, except x0.

## 5. Milestone acceptance criteria

Every milestone also requires: `make lint` clean (Verilator `--lint-only -Wall` and
Yosys `read_verilog -sv` on all of rtl/), `make test` green, results committed under
results/ with the commit hash, and the git tag.

**M1 — single-cycle RV32I (`corv32_sc`) + cocotb.**
1. cocotb unit tests pass:
   - `corv32_alu`: every op, 20,000 random vectors per op plus corner values {0, 1, −1,
     INT_MIN, INT_MAX, shift amounts 0/31}, checked against a Python model;
   - `corv32_decode`: one directed case per instruction, plus 100,000 random 32-bit words
     whose legal/illegal verdict and fields are checked against a Python decoder written
     from the spec tables;
   - `corv32_regfile` and `corv32_lsu`: exhaustive over size × addr[1:0] × signedness.
2. All 37 RV32I base instructions have self-checking directed assembly tests in
   `sw/tests/rv32i/` that pass on `corv32_sc`.
3. riscv-formal on `corv32_sc` (isa rv32i) passes: insn, reg, pc_fwd, pc_bwd, ill,
   causal and unique, at depth ≥ 10. This is the walking-skeleton proof.

**M2 — five-stage pipeline, forwarding, hazards, branches (RV32I subset of `corv32_core`).**
1. The M1 directed suite passes on `corv32_core`, with the cocotb bus model in two modes:
   zero-wait, and random wait (gnt and rvalid each delayed 0–3 cycles at random, 10 seeds).
2. Directed hazard tests cover each forwarding source (MEM, WB, regfile write-through) ×
   {rs1, rs2, store data, branch operand}, load-use on rs1 and rs2, back-to-back taken
   branches, and a branch right after a load.
3. Cycle-exact tests, in the zero-wait mode: 1000 independent ALU ops retire in 1000 + c
   cycles, with c a fixed fill latency stated in the test; one load-use costs exactly
   +1 cycle; one taken branch or jump costs exactly +1 cycle; a not-taken branch costs 0.
4. riscv-formal (isa rv32i) on `corv32_core` passes the DESIGN §9.2 checks restricted to
   rv32i, at the §9.2 depths.

**M3 — M extension, CSRs, traps, interrupts.**
1. Unit tests: `corv32_mul` and `corv32_div` pass a spec corner table (div by 0,
   INT_MIN/−1, sign combinations) plus 100,000 random vectors per op against Python. SBY
   *prove* (unbounded, k-induction) shows `corv32_div #(WIDTH=8)` and
   `corv32_mul #(FAST=0, WIDTH=8)` match the spec arithmetic for all inputs.
2. Directed tests trigger every exception cause in §4.5 and every interrupt (MSI, MTI,
   MEI), in direct and vectored mode, plus nested-disable (MIE cleared on entry) and MRET
   restore. They also exercise the CSR legal/illegal table of §4.2 entry by entry, and
   the counter write-precedence rules.
3. riscv-formal (isa rv32im, ALTOPS) passes the complete DESIGN §9.2 list. This is E1.1.

**M4 — verification.** E1.1, E1.2 and E1.3 hold. Coverage report produced
(DESIGN §9.5): line coverage of rtl/core outside `CORV32_RVFI` regions ≥ 95%, every
uncovered line waived with a reason in results/coverage/WAIVERS.md, and every functional
bin hit. The mutation study (C1) has run, and its kill matrix is in results/mutation/.

**M5 — SoC and Verilator model.**
1. `build/sim/Vcorv32_soc` boots from the simulated SPI flash: the boot ROM copies the
   image, and "hello" is printed over the UART TX monitor.
2. SoC tests pass: CLINT timer interrupt at a programmed mtimecmp; MSI via msip; MEI via
   UART RX with IER = 1 (harness injects a byte on `uart_rx`); GPIO out→in loopback; a
   read of an unmapped address gives a load access fault.
3. E1.2 and E1.3 have been run through this same SoC model in bench mode.
4. E1.4: CoreMark/MHz ≥ 2.00 measured as in §3.

**M6 — synthesis.** `make syn` produces results/syn/*.csv (design, seed, Fmax, LUT4,
FF, LUTRAM, DP16KD, DSP, commit). It covers corv32 (default and the 8 C3
configurations), PicoRV32 ×2 and VexRiscv ×3, with 10 seeds each, plus the
`corv32_soc` ULX3S top (place and route plus bitstream). Tables are generated by script.
The on-board run is an entry in HARDWARE_TODO.md.

**M7 — mcugrad.** The mcugrad-generated `mnist_cnn` C (int8, single file) runs on
`corv32_soc` in Verilator. For the first 100 test images, the int8 logits equal the
host-compiled reference byte for byte (0 mismatches). We report cycles per inference
(mean, min and max over the 100 images) and time per inference = mean cycles / SoC median
Fmax from M6, labelled as derived from simulation. A measurement on the board is an entry
in HARDWARE_TODO.md.

## 6. Pass/fail bookkeeping

`results/` holds one JSON per gate (`e1_formal.json`, `e1_riscof.json`,
`e1_lockstep.json`, `e1_coremark.json`, `c1_matrix.csv`). Each has the commit, tool
versions, seeds and raw counts. The paper macros are generated from these files only.

## 7. Threats to validity and limitations (to be carried into the paper)

1. **RISCOF is deprecated upstream** in favour of ACT 4.0 (Sail reference). We use RISCOF
   + riscv-arch-test 3.9.1 + Spike because the brief names RISCOF (DECISIONS D4). We
   state the version, and make no ACT4 claim.
2. **riscv-formal is bounded.** BMC at depth d only proves no counterexample within d
   cycles of reset. Funck et al. (FDL 2023) show riscv-formal has holes. This is why
   claim C1 exists.
3. **ALTOPS.** The real multiplier and divider datapaths are not covered by riscv-formal.
   They are covered by unit proofs at WIDTH=8, unit tests, RISCOF M tests and lockstep.
4. **Bus faults are not formally checked.** The formal wrapper ties `err` to 0. Fault
   paths are covered by directed tests and lockstep (accesses to 0x4000_0000).
5. **Lockstep exclusions** (DESIGN §9.4) are behaviours where Spike and corv32 may
   legally differ: counter and time reads, marchid, mhpmevent, mcountinhibit, misa
   writes, MMIO devices other than the CLINT msip/mtimecmp, external interrupts and bus
   wait states. Lockstep runs the SoC with zero-wait memory, so wait-state behaviour is
   covered only by cocotb random-wait runs and by formal.
6. **CoreMark comes from simulation.** It is not EEMBC-certified, and the 10-s rule is
   met only in simulated time (§3). Results are flag-dependent; flags are fixed in §3.
7. **Baseline fairness.** No pregenerated VexRiscv variant is cache-less RV32IM, and
   regenerating one needs sbt/Java, which is outside the toolchain. Its caches inflate
   LUT/BRAM, so BRAM is reported separately. PicoRV32's interrupt scheme is
   non-standard. Baselines get ideal memories in the CoreMark harness.
8. **Mutation validity.** Netlist-level single-point mutants are not real design bugs,
   which is why B also contains 20 realistic hand-written bugs. Equivalent mutants are
   triaged by hand, and the triage is published.
9. **Prior art.** This is not the first core to combine these methods
   (PRIOR_ART §3.3). The novelty is limited to C1–C3.
